feedback: Expected: rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours).
'Change of state' = the same material in a different state, e.g. ice (solid) melting to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezing back.

If the learner says the balloon has 'nothing' or 'just air': make the gas tangible as a demonstration — squeeze the sealed balloon or fan the air onto a face so it can be felt; this shows the gas is really there and takes up space, filling its container (the 'push' you feel is the trapped air, not the definition — the point is a gas is a real material that fills the space).
If 'solid' is taken to mean strong/big, 'gas' only petrol/fumes, or 'liquid' any wet thing: re-anchor each word to BEHAVIOUR (shape and container), not size, smell or wetness.
Listen for the words used correctly in context ('fills its container', 'keeps its shape'), not merely recited; naming the trio alone (recitation) is not enough.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct, meaningful USE of the behaviour-vocabulary in context (including tricky cases) shows genuine understanding, not recitation of the three words.
learnerActions: Name whether each of several things is solid, liquid or gas AND describe HOW it behaves: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.
Explain what 'change of state' means, using ice as the example (ice melting to water, or water freezing back), including what happens to ice on a warm day.

Answer probing questions: Is the air in the balloon solid, liquid or gas — how can you tell it's really there? Sand pours like a drink — is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain. Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid — what makes it hard to decide?
activities.title: Use the words like a scientist (checkpoint)
